Micromanaging, zero error

Challenge What happens What to do
Micromanaging The leader keeps correcting every small thing. Trust people to take responsibility and correct themselves.
Zero error syndrome The leader expects a perfect result with no error. So they don’t delegate, or keep interfering after delegating. Delegate and let people work.
Responsibility without resources People get a job but not the authority or resources to do it. Empower them — give responsibility with authority.
Unclear roles Two people step on each other’s toes. The leader must define roles and responsibilities clearly, and create understanding where roles overlap.
Personal vs professional life Problems at home affect work, and the other way round. Good leaders manage both well.

Lesson 1: Uphold your core

blocks.html: Values are what is most important and meaningful to you. They are your principles, ideals and standards — an honour code you follow even when nobody is watching.

blocks.html: Values shape your actions, behaviour, attitudes, decisions and choices. When you feel lost, they work like a guiding compass. They help you be your real, authentic self.

blocks.html: From the slide:
blocks.text: From the slide:

  • Values guide thoughts, plans, decisions, choices, actions.

blocks.text:
Core values are non-negotiable . Core values are a guiding compass for individuals,
groups or organisations. Values guide thoughts, plans, decisions, choices,
actions . Clearly define the values of yourself, groups or
organisation. Uphold your core values — do not
compromise them.

blocks.caption:
Core values work like a compass
when you feel lost.

blocks.html:
Lecture example — Lt Col Jayakumar’s three core values

  1. Honesty — there are no shades of grey. You are either honest or not.
  2. Adaptability — in the army, he had to adapt to deserts and high-altitude places. His hardest change was moving from the army uniform to civilian life at IIT Madras.
  3. Being responsible for his command — not just himself. A young officer leads about 30 soldiers; later, 800–1,000.

The firing practice story (Kargil, around 1998–99): During artillery practice, an observer asked to “add 800” metres. The safety officer said “drop 400” because shells might go over the hill. As officer in charge, he said: “I am responsible — fire 800.” Later, three shells landed near a village, and locals complained to the collector. He went himself to face them. Luckily, there was little damage, and red flags had warned people. His lesson: know your job and boundaries, and stand by your subordinates who acted in good faith.

Lesson 2: Know

blocks.html: Know what is in your control and what is not. Then you can focus your energy where it has the most effect. You save time, energy and mind space.

Know what is in your control and what is not . Then you can focus your energy where it has the

blocks.caption:
Sphere of
control (inside), sphere of influence (middle), sphere of concern
(outside).

blocks.html:
Sphere What is in it What to do
Sphere of control (centre) Your mind, body, potential, time and energy Focus here most. You can change these.
Sphere of influence (middle) People close to you — family, friends, peers, your students Outside your control. You can guide them when needed; otherwise stay out.
Sphere of concern or interest (outside) Other groups, the economy, world events, politics, war Outside your control. Affects you indirectly. Find helpful ways to respond — but spend the least time here.

Lesson

  • If a choice isn’t working, explore other choices and make a new one.
  • You don’t wait for someone else to fix it. You take the initiative.
  • You seek help and build a support system. Asking for help is a sign of strength, not weakness.

blocks.caption:
“I only know this, so I
won’t try” vs “Let me learn, explore and partner.”

blocks.html:
Lecture example — Prof. Kartic: from board games to digital games He designed board and card games and believed they were the best. He also believed “I cannot design digital games”. So he didn’t even try to understand some customers’ problems. That is a fixed mindset. Weeks and months passed with no work.

Then the pandemic came. People could not meet to play board games. He was forced to go digital. First he just copied board games into digital form. Slowly he learnt that the two worlds are different.

He also broke another belief: “I must do everything alone.” He started partnering with digital game companies. A whole new world opened up.

His shift: from “I know it all, I want quick results” → to “I am here to learn, explore and partner.” Now he works in a zone of learning and possibilities.

blocks.caption:
To-do list, easy start, energy
boosters and a short rest to recharge.

blocks.html:
Lecture example — Prof. Sivakumar: “I don’t manage time, I manage myself”

  • Prioritise: what is urgent, what is important.
  • Make it easy to start: he put his bike key inside the meeting file, so he couldn’t forget the file. When writing a paper, he stops mid-sentence, so the next day his mind wants to finish it — and he gets into flow.
  • Love what you do: many things are not in your hands, so train yourself to love the work you have.
  • Recharge: a 45-minute nap (siesta) in the afternoon; meditation in the morning; a short stroll or a little music to break monotony.
  • Track energy: use the fresh morning for creative work.

blocks.html:

blocks.text: Introduction

blocks.html:
• Three parts, all starting with you.
  • True leaders create more leaders, not followers; followers come automatically.
  • Leading yourself builds empathy and makes you the example.
  • Challenges: micromanaging · zero error syndrome (expecting perfection, so not delegating or interfering) · responsibility without authority/resources · unclear roles · balancing personal and professional life.

Three parts, all starting with you . True leaders create more leaders , not followers;
followers come automatically. Leading yourself builds empathy and makes you the example . Challenges: micromanaging · zero error

Part 1: Lead
yourself from within (6 lessons)

blocks.html:
# Lesson Key points
1 Uphold your core values Non-negotiable; a guiding compass; do what is right, not what is easy. Col: honesty, adaptability, responsibility for his command (“I am responsible — fire 800”). Corruption isn’t only money — a teacher who doesn’t teach is corrupt.
2 Know your spheres of responsibility Control (mind, body, potential, time, energy) → Influence (family, friends, peers) → Concern (other groups, economy, world events). Covey: focus on control and your impact grows. Be proactive: “I’m doing this — is it okay?” not “Tell me what to do”.
3 Exercise your power of choice Space between stimulus and response (Covey). Choice to say yes/no, explore, seek help, build a support system. Choices bring responsibility. Dean’s “no” to a disciplined student — conduct over winning.
4 Take responsibility/ownership Stop playing victim or blaming. Seek help = strength. Victim (react, compete, win–lose, blame) vs Owner (create, collaborate, win–win, calm, resourceful). Respons-ibility = choose your response.
5 Play to your full potential Put in 100%; play to strengths; know weaknesses; strengths have downsides, weaknesses have upsides (extrovert may miss details; introvert listens well).
6 Invest in yourself Self-growth, self-care, self-worth, self-love. The event is not the self — failing ≠ being a failure.

Part 2: Lead
yourself to lead others (9 lessons)

blocks.html:
# Lesson Key points
1 Cultivate a growth mindset Overcome adversity; obstacles → opportunities. Kartic: “I can’t do digital games” → explored and partnered.
2 Manage time and energy To-do lists; prioritise; make it easy to start (bike key in the file; stop mid-sentence); love what you do; energy drainers vs boosters; recharge (siesta, meditation, stroll). “I manage myself, not time.”
3 Focus on the one thing Gary Keller: one thing that makes everything else easier. Write goals; goals support each other. Sivakumar’s one thing: joy.
4 Communicate effectively & listen actively Words of power; body language; speak so others listen; listen actively; silence and pause; solitude. Hearing ≠ listening. Know your job, their job, and the shared goal.
5 Be emotionally resilient Emotional intelligence; EQ valued over IQ. Identify triggers; regulate emotions; self-awareness via reflection, mentors, meditation, journaling.
6 Embrace change Expect, monitor, adapt quickly, learn lessons. Student → corporate → entrepreneur.
7 Manage conflict Inner conflict: values, expectations, perceptions, inner chatter. Say NO; clear agreements; reframe your lens; be your own inner coach. Creates psychological safety.
8 Delegate effectively Pick team players who can lead themselves; mutual trust; align values; define roles; empower; psychological safety.
9 Be a collaborative leader Open, non-judgmental; equal opportunity; divergent thinking before converging; listen–understand–act; tools and processes. Example: Sundar Pichai.
